title: The Legislature
hook: The branch that makes the law is also where a society argues out loud — the legislature turns competing interests into binding rules through debate and votes.
key_points: The legislature is the branch that makes laws, approves budgets, and represents the public.
It usually also scrutinizes the executive — questioning ministers and investigating policy.
Many legislatures are bicameral: two chambers must agree, adding a check within the branch.
Members are typically elected, making the legislature the most directly representative branch.
content_html: The legislature is the branch of government charged with making the law. But its work is broader than passing statutes: it typically approves the government's budget — the "power of the purse" — represents citizens by channeling their interests into national debate, and scrutinizes the executive by questioning ministers, holding hearings, and investigating how policy is carried out. Because its members are usually elected, it is the branch most directly tied to the public, which is why it sits at the heart of representative government.
extra_html: Legislatures vary in shape. Many are bicameral, divided into two chambers — often a larger house representing the population and a second chamber representing regions or providing a chamber of review. Requiring both to agree before a law passes builds a check into the branch itself and slows hasty decisions. Others are unicameral, with a single chamber, which is simpler and faster. Encyclopaedia Britannica notes that the legislature's relationship to the executive also differs by system: in parliamentary systems the executive is drawn from and answerable to the legislature, while in presidential systems the two are separately elected. Across these designs, the legislature's combination of lawmaking, budgeting, representation, and oversight makes it a central engine of democratic accountability.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: How a Bill Becomes a Law
related.hook: An idea becomes binding law only after a journey: drafting, committee review, debate, votes, and final approval.

related.title: The Executive
related.hook: Laws don't enforce themselves. The executive is the branch that runs the state day to day — carrying out the law, commanding the bureaucracy, and acting in a crisis.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core job of a legislature?
flashcards.back_html: To make laws — and typically to approve budgets, represent the public, and scrutinize the executive.

flashcards.prompt: What does it mean for a legislature to be 'bicameral'?

choices.text: It has two chambers that must both agree to pass a law
It meets only twice a year
It shares its building with the courts

flashcards.explanation_html: A bicameral legislature splits into two chambers; requiring both to agree adds a check on lawmaking within the branch itself.

flashcards.prompt: Why is the legislature often called the most representative branch?

choices.text: Its members are typically elected directly by the public
It has the most employees of any branch

flashcards.explanation_html: Because legislators are usually chosen in elections, the legislature is the branch most directly accountable to voters.
